performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
intro: “Samuel” Goldenberg und “Schmuÿle”, marked Andante, is the sixth movement of Pictures at an Exhibition and portrays two figures, here in Ravel’s orchestration. Goldenberg has a unison melody and Schmuÿle a stream of repeated notes; later Ravel sets one muted trumpet against the whole string section.

sections.label: A · Goldenberg theme in unison
sections.mNote: Low woodwinds and strings play in unison.

sections.label: B · Schmuÿle, repeated muted-trumpet notes
sections.mNote: A muted trumpet repeats its phrase above woodwind chords.

sections.label: A′ · Both themes combined
sections.mNote: Goldenberg’s low tune sounds beneath Schmuÿle’s repeated notes.

sections.label: Coda · Con dolore, then emphatic close
sections.mNote: The music slows, marked con dolore, before the emphatic close.

cues.title: Goldenberg’s theme in unison
cues.text: Goldenberg’s phrase is broad and heavily accented. Low woodwinds and strings play it in unison, without a separate accompaniment. The line includes a leap from G♭ to A, an augmented second.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 1–8; Peter Laki describes the unison and augmented second: https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition-mussorgsky. Instrumentation follows Joanna Wyld’s Philharmonia guide; Ravel attribution for this recording remains inferred.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Schmuÿle, muted trumpet
cues.text: Schmuÿle enters on a muted trumpet, which repeats notes in quick groups. The score changes to Andantino.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 9–18, Andantino and repeated-note figures; muted trumpet: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, 7 April 2022, p. 7: https://philharmonia-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2022/04/07.04.22_RFH-online.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two Hartmann portraits, Mussorgsky’s collection
cues.text: Mussorgsky owned both of the Hartmann drawings behind this scene. One showed a wealthy Jewish man in a fur hat, the other a poor Jewish man from Sandomierz, the Polish town where Hartmann spent a month in 1868. Mussorgsky put the two separate portraits together in one movement.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, Boston Symphony programme note, identifies the drawings, their ownership and Hartmann’s 1868 stay in Sandomierz: https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition

cues.title: Ending in Ravel’s orchestration
cues.text: Mussorgsky’s piano piece ends on a long final note. In Ravel’s scoring Goldenberg dismisses Schmuÿle more abruptly. A warmer idea is cut short by an emphatic ending.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, Boston Symphony programme note: Mussorgsky ends with a long note, but Ravel has Goldenberg dismiss Schmuyle more abruptly (https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition). Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, p. 7: a warmer idea is swiftly curtailed by the emphatic ending (https://philharmonia-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2022/04/07.04.22_RFH-online.pdf).

transitions.title: Muted trumpet enters over held D♭
transitions.how: Goldenberg’s phrase ends on D♭. That note is held beneath the next passage, and the melody moves to a high register in repeated notes. In Ravel’s scoring it goes to a muted trumpet over woodwind chords. Mussorgsky changes the marking from Andante to Andantino.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 8–10, held D♭ and Andantino: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/MussorgskyM/pictures-at-an-exhibition/pictures-at-an-exhibition-lys/two-jews.ly. Scoring: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia guide.

transitions.title: Goldenberg’s theme returns under Schmuÿle
transitions.how: Andante, grave brings back Goldenberg’s tune in the lower parts. Schmuÿle’s repeated D♭ continues above it. Ravel gives Goldenberg’s theme to the strings and keeps Schmuÿle’s on one muted trumpet, so the two themes sound together.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 18–25; Peter Laki describes the simultaneous string and muted-trumpet themes in the Cleveland Orchestra programme note.

transitions.title: Fermata and slowing before the close
transitions.to: Coda · Con dolore, then emphatic close
transitions.how: An accented chord cuts off the repeated notes, and a fermata holds the silence that follows. Over B♭ in the bass, the next phrase is marked con dolore — with sorrow — and slows (poco ritard in Lamm’s edition, bars 25–29). The clipped figures of the opening return for an emphatic final dismissal.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 25–29: fermata, B♭ bass and poco ritard con dolore; Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note describes Ravel’s shortened final dismissal.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive; conductor unknown)
fields.note: The Commons page names no performer (“see Musopen for performance author information”). The Free Music Archive album of 15 tracks by the Skidmore College Orchestra lists a track of the same title and length (2:10; this file is 2:08), and the Internet Archive item for the first Promenade credits the same orchestra. The identification of this file with that track rests on title and length; the Musopen performer page was not opened. Conductor: unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

composer.epithet: Composer who could make a singer sound like a frightened child, a drunken monk or a tsar who could no longer bear his own thoughts.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition with Mily Balakirev, outside the conservatory
Guards officer until 1858; later a clerk in the Forestry Department and Government Control
Borodin, Cui, Balakirev, Rimsky-Korsakov; Vladimir Stasov and Viktor Hartmann
Boris Godunov, unfinished operas, three song cycles, Pictures at an Exhibition
composer.background:
When Borodin met Mussorgsky at a Saint Petersburg military hospital in 1856, the seventeen-year-old officer was immaculate, with a close-fitting uniform, polished manners and well-kept hands. He played extracts from Il trovatore and La traviata at the piano while admirers gathered round. Twenty-five years later, in another hospital, Repin painted the portrait that became his most familiar likeness. It shows a man in a dressing gown, his hair in disorder and his eyes still alert.

Mussorgsky was born at Karevo, on his family’s estate. His mother taught him the piano, and his nurse’s stories prompted the improvisations he remembered from childhood. At ten he was sent to school in Saint Petersburg, where he studied piano with Anton Gerke. He entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852 and received a commission in the Preobrazhensky Regiment in 1856. His father paid for the publication of his first piano piece, a polka.
